We use a stochastic SIRDS model throughout the examples. People move between
**susceptible**, **infected**, **recovered** and **dead** compartments; recovered
people can become susceptible again.

The inputs are the initial infected fraction (`I0`) and four rates:
transmission (`beta`), recovery (`gamma`), waning immunity (`omega`) and death
(`mu`). The outputs are the four population counts at each time step.

## Run the simulator

This example fixes all inputs, uses a population of 1,000 and takes daily steps.
Changing the random seed gives a different realisation of the same process.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from metis.datasets.sirds import simulate_sirds

parameters = dict(I0=0.005, beta=0.4, gamma=0.1, omega=0.02, mu=0.01)
trajectories = np.array([
    simulate_sirds(**parameters, N=1000, T=120, dt=1, seed=seed)
    for seed in range(20)
])
print("Shape (realisations, compartments, time points):", trajectories.shape)
print("Population conserved:", bool(np.all(trajectories.sum(axis=1) == 1000)))
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "SIRDS: 20 simulations at the same parameter values. The variation is from stochastic process draws, not fitted parameter uncertainty."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(11, 3), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for i, (label, colour) in enumerate(zip(
    ["Susceptible", "Infected", "Recovered", "Dead"],
    ["#2E86AB", "#C73E1D", "#6A994E", "#C21B8A"],
)):
    axes[i].plot(np.arange(121), trajectories[:, i, :].T,
                 color=colour, alpha=0.35, linewidth=1)
    axes[i].set(title=label, xlabel="Day")
axes[0].set_ylabel("People")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

A deterministic surrogate learns one trajectory for these inputs. A stochastic
surrogate can generate multiple trajectories, aiming to reproduce the
variation as well as the average.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Time stepping"}
The simulator uses binomial draws for infection and waning, and a multinomial
draw for recovery, death or remaining infected. Recovery/death probabilities
are `1 - exp(-rate * dt)` and must sum to at most one. This discrete approximation
preserves the population; it is not an exact continuous-time simulation.
:::
